title: #[\Override] attribute
summary: PHP 8.3 added the #[\Override] attribute, which marks a method as intentionally overriding a method declared by a parent class or an implemented interface.
new_code_policy: On a PHP 8.3+ floor, add #[\Override] to every method that is meant to override a parent class or interface method, so the engine can verify the relationship at compile time.
existing_code_policy: Once the project's PHP floor reaches 8.3, add #[\Override] to existing overriding methods incrementally; a genuinely mismatched "override" (typo, renamed or removed parent method) then surfaces as a fatal compile-time error instead of silently defining an unrelated new method.
guideline: Mark every method that overrides a parent class or interface method with #[\Override].
details: PHP 8.3 introduced the #[\Override] attribute (RFC marking_overriden_methods). Applying it to a method declares that the method is expected to override a method from a parent class, an abstract parent, or an interface it implements. If no such ancestor method exists, PHP raises a compile-time fatal error instead of silently letting the method stand as an unrelated addition. This turns a class of refactor-time drift bugs — a parent method renamed, narrowed in visibility, or removed while a subclass still assumes it exists — into an error the engine catches immediately rather than a bug found later at runtime.
notes: PHP 8.5 extended #[\Override]'s allowed targets to properties (RFC override_properties). This is a scope extension of the same attribute for an already-covered construct, not a second introduction: it does not change introduced_in and is not a second sources[] entry.

behavior_change_risk is "low", not "none": adding the attribute to a method that is not actually an override (e.g. because the parent method was already gone) converts previously-silent drift into a fatal compile-time error — a deliberate and desirable behavior change, but a real one for a blind mechanical addition.
